1:
Gill dates the episode after the two Syrian campaigns, when Ahab had conquered and had then let Benhadad go free, a blasphemer unpunished. Clarke adds that the Septuagint reverses this chapter and the one before it, so that the murder of Naboth precedes the war with Benhadad, and that Josephus follows the same order. Where the vineyard lay is harder. Delitzsch, weighing the title king of Samaria against a plot sited in Jezreel, concludes that Jezreel, the modern Zerin, was no more than a summer seat.

Ellicott turns that tension into an open question. The Greek drops the words which was in Jezreel and sets the ground beside Ahab's threshing-floor at Samaria, using the term rendered void place at 1 Kings 22:10; the Vulgate reads who was for which was. Three things favour Samaria: the emphatic sentence of verse 19 is declared fulfilled at that city's pool in 1 Kings 22:38, everything the king does here seems done there, and verse 18 says as much if taken literally. Against them stand the received reading, the obvious force of his city later in the chapter, and the plot of ground at Jezreel in 2 Kings 9:25-26. He judges Samaria the likelier and grants that the discrepancy cannot be cleared up.

The offer itself was courteous: silver, or a better vineyard in exchange. Gill takes the herb garden for a kitchen plot, or a flower garden, or with Kimchi both, and guesses Ahab caught the taste from the Syrians, whose horticulture Pliny praised. Clarke and Henry agree the king was asking what no Israelite could grant. Land might be sold or mortgaged, but it reverted at the jubilee (Leviticus 25:25-28); what Ahab wanted was a permanent transfer, and to tempt a subject into it was, Clarke says, high iniquity. He observes too that despotic as these kings were, none dared simply seize a field: that would have broken the very constitution they existed to administer as God's vicegerents, and no Jewish monarch could alter an old statute or frame a new one. Henry sharpens the irony: having tamely let slip his chance to enlarge the realm after beating the Syrians, Ahab now strains every nerve to enlarge a garden, as though being penny wise could atone for being pound foolish.

Delitzsch presses that Naboth was not merely free to refuse but bound to, the sale of a patrimony being forbidden at Numbers 36:7. Henry, who calls Canaan peculiarly God's own country and Israel his tenants, reports the conjecture that Naboth saw his acre as an earnest of the heavenly portion and would not risk the greater by parting with the lesser; Gill, noting the man was prosperous and under no compulsion to sell, counts him among the seven thousand who never bowed to Baal and thinks the crown already bore him a grudge. Only Ellicott hears something ungracious in the answer, a curtness that condemns as well as declines, though what it declined was not merely lawful but right.

All of them linger on what follows. Ahab went home, turned his face to the wall as mourners do, and would not eat. Delitzsch, borrowing Seb. Schmidt's phrase about those who shun conversation and even the sight of others, reads the sulk as proof of a man sold under sin who lacked only the energy to act his heart out. Clarke is blunter: master of ten-twelfths of the land, and wretched because one poor plot was not added to it. Ellicott calls it the temper of a spoilt child, and the natural seedplot of crime once a stronger wickedness takes it in hand. Henry finds discontent both its own punishment and its own parent, since Paul was content in a prison and this man miserable in a palace.
5:
Gill has Jezebel simply noticing her husband's low spirits and wishing to relieve them; Henry sees the comfort as a pretence for feeding his pride and blowing the coals of his corruption. Both fasten on what Ahab left out of his account. Naboth had said he may not sell; the king reports him as saying he will not, turning a scruple of conscience into mere peevishness. Delitzsch reads the reply as irony, the pronoun thrown forward for emphasis and the Greek treating it as a question: dost thou exercise royal power in Israel? Then her offer, made because he has not the nerve himself.

Henry allows the taunt a good sense as well as a bad one. It might mean that a prince shames his crown by sinking under so small a loss, and that a man who cannot govern his own passions is hardly fit to govern a nation. What she meant was the other thing: use the prerogative, seize what courtesy will not fetch, and failing that, lend me your name. Clarke reaches the same place. If Naboth may refuse and Ahab may not take, Naboth is the greater man of the two, and this is the native speech of despotism. Ellicott hears Lady Macbeth in the scorn, a wife impatient with one who lets I dare not wait upon I would, and observes that the invitation to eat and be merry concedes the very self-indulgence Elijah had played upon at 1 Kings 18:41. This husband is fit to desire and to revel; acting, for good or ill, falls to bolder spirits.

Over the signet the witnesses converge uncomfortably. Gill assumes the king lent it without being told the plan; Clarke says flatly that she counterfeited his authority by his own consent. Delitzsch explains the instrument, a seal bearing the royal name and stamped rather than signed, as Arabs, Turks and Persians still do, which gave a letter the force of a command. Ellicott presses hardest: because such a seal was carried on the person, its use implies Ahab knew something was being done in his name and took care not to ask what.

Gill reports Kimchi's reading that proclaim a fast means convene a court, and backs it, since Jezebel can have had little notion of fasting and a genuine humiliation would hardly be cried in one town only. Ellicott keeps the fast but gives it work beyond disguise, as a hint that some hidden offence had drawn danger on the city, which prepares the way for the charge; he finds set Naboth on high equally double, either mock honour or the lifting up of the head for trial as at Genesis 40:20, and notes that the whole design presumes the people had returned to at least an outward keeping of the law. Henry's verdict is the harshest: no wickedness is so vile that religion has not at some time been made a cover for it, and none so monstrous as one carried through with the forms of a legal process.

Two accusers were required (Deuteronomy 17:6), and Gill calls the pair men who had thrown off the yoke and would swear to anything. The wording of the charge is itself disputed. Clarke reports Parkhurst's contention that the verb never means to curse, so that the accusation ran rather that Naboth had blessed the false gods, a capital matter under Deuteronomy 17:2-7; he prefers the plainer sense and warns that letting one word carry two opposite meanings is dangerous. Ellicott takes it as to renounce rather than to blaspheme, though stoning followed as for blasphemy proper (Leviticus 24:16). Henry explains why both God and king stand in the indictment: profaning the one cost a man his life, treason against the other cost him his land, and it was land that Ahab wanted.
11:
What surprises Gill is not the queen's invention, nor that the town held men who would swear to anything, but that the elders and nobles, the magistrates themselves, were so far gone; idolatry, once it prevails, strips away every sense of humanity and justice. Ellicott reads the same compliance as typical of the baser forms of organised Eastern despotism, which will not kill by open violence without some cause shown, yet can always poison the springs of justice and commit murder under legal form. He adds a reason peculiar to Israel: where the crown was reckoned only God's deputy, subject in theory to the supreme law under the manner of the kingdom (1 Samuel 10:25), the need to dress crime in legal clothing would be felt the more. Henry notes that they neither raised a difficulty nor met with one, whether from fear of the queen or hatred of the man's piety.

Gill reads the posture of the two hirelings as significant. They sat facing the accused, the settled arrangement for accuser and accused, as it later was among the Romans. He observes that Josephus makes them three, while the Targum and every ancient version keep them at two. Ellicott, on the carrying out of the city, gives the usual reason, that blood must not pollute the place, and raises the possibility that the execution happened on the dead man's own ground, in the coveted vineyard itself.

How the land then passed is a question all the witnesses feel. Clarke infers from 2 Kings 9:26, where the Lord speaks of the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons, that the whole family was destroyed, leaving the ground to escheat with no heir at law; Ellicott says the same and adds that even had there been heirs, a traitor's property would naturally fall to the crown, though the Law enacts nothing of the kind. Delitzsch supplies the missing principle: since a blasphemer's goods were forfeited to the Lord as cherem (Deuteronomy 13:16), a traitor's were held forfeit to the king, a rule implied in the idea of treason rather than written anywhere. Henry offers both titles in turn, failure of blood if the sons were dead and forfeiture by crime if they were not, and thinks that if neither would serve, Jezebel's will would have done instead.

Ahab could have sent an officer to enter for him. Henry points out that he went himself, and went in some state, since Jehu recalled long afterwards that he and Bidkar had ridden behind him that day (2 Kings 9:25). Ellicott finds it wholly in character that the king asked nothing about how the owner died, careful to be innocent of the knowledge while tacitly applauding the deed: the guilt is his wife's, the fruit his own. He records a curious Greek insertion here, that Ahab rent his clothes and put on sackcloth, which he grants is true to such a nature, a spasm of horror soon salved and then set aside, but judges poorly attested and probably drawn back from verse 27. Clarke admits that by what rites possession was taken nobody now knows.

Henry closes the section with a symmetry worth keeping. Orders came from Samaria to the elders of Jezreel, and they murdered Naboth; orders came later from Jezreel to the elders of Samaria, and they murdered the seventy sons of Ahab (2 Kings 10:6-7). Rulers who debauch the consciences of their inferior magistrates may find the wheel come round, for men who will do one cruel thing at command will do another against the man who commanded it. Meanwhile might prevails against right, and the divine patience that permits it is, he says, wonderful, God keeping silence while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself (Habakkuk 1:13).
17:
Elijah has been absent since the call of Elisha, and Gill admits nobody knows where or at what; lesser prophets had carried the messages of the interval, and he guesses that during the Syrian war the Tishbite was founding or reviving the schools whose pupils appear later. The Targum names what now comes to him the word of prophecy. Ellicott makes the silence deliberate: the merely political business of the preceding chapter, so weighty in the world's eyes, drew him out not at all, and he returns for the higher duty of rebuking a crime and avenging blood that Eastern tyranny would think a trifle. Henry sets the two errands side by side. A prophet of lower rank had been sent to Ahab with kindness before the battle; the father of the prophets is sent to convict him of murder.

Clarke dates the meeting to the day after the killing, reasoning back from 2 Kings 9:26. Henry dwells on where it happens. Sentence is read in the vineyard itself, at the moment of entry, because entering avowed the whole business and made the king an accessory after the fact; a man taken in the act feels the conviction the harder. The geography stays contested. Gill takes the phrase about Samaria for Ahab's seat, adding that Benjamin of Tudela claimed traces of the palace were still visible; Delitzsch renders it who dwells in Samaria, since the king was plainly at Jezreel when the prophet met him; Ellicott holds the words almost meaningless unless they say Ahab was then in Samaria, and calls any softening of them an explaining away.

The charge is two words long. Gill notes that the Vulgate and the Arabic, with Joseph Kimchi and Ben Melech, drop the question mark and read it flat as an accusation, and that the killing is laid at the king's door because his coveting caused it, his wife contrived it, and he very likely knew and consented to more than the record says. Ellicott admires the brevity: it shames the subterfuge of shifting everything onto Jezebel, exposes what the crime was actually for, and leaves its object with nothing to say before sentence falls.

Over that sentence the witnesses divide sharply. Clarke holds it vain to look for a literal fulfilment, since the penitence of verse 29 deferred the stroke; dogs did lick this king's blood, but at the pool of Samaria where his chariot was washed after Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:38), though some make that the very spot of the stoning, and the word touching his son came true to the letter when Jehoram's body was flung into Naboth's ground. He compares Orestes sending Aegisthus to die where he had killed. Ellicott rejects the whole of this. The emphasis of even thy blood, he argues, forbids any reading that finds fulfilment in Jehoram, and verse 29 cannot be invoked, because it is not this clause of the doom that repentance postpones.

Ahab's greeting is read several ways at once. Gill's account of the name is the simplest, that the prophet dealt faithfully and reproved him. Delitzsch rejects the Vulgate and Luther rendering, hast thou ever found me thine enemy, for the plainer dost thou meet me again, and explains the epithet as an attempt to blunt the threat by making it look like private spite. Ellicott hears dismay mixed with excuse, the same evasion as the cry about troubling Israel at 1 Kings 18:17, and answers it: the prophet came not from enmity but because this man had sold himself and was now a slave where he should have been a king. Clarke glosses the selling from Romans 7:14. Henry sharpens the comparison instead, for Paul was sold under sin as a captive against his will, whereas Ahab made the sale himself, of choice.
21:
Henry first closes off the two escapes. It would not serve for Ahab to plead that the law killed Naboth, since perverted justice is the worst injustice of all; nor that the prosecution was none of his doing, since it was done to please him and he had shown himself pleased. He killed, because he took possession. Take the garden and you take the guilt with it: the land passes with its encumbrance.

The doom itself falls in stages. Gill hears the first clause of it as personal, a violent end for the king himself, and notes the bitterness of that in a man with seventy sons to carry his name. Delitzsch sets out the rest as one continuous oracle, and Henry supplies the precedents. To be made like the houses of Jeroboam and of Baasha was no vague comparison; Gill recalls that both lines were rooted out entirely, and the very terms of this curse, dogs in the city and birds in the open country, had already been spoken against each of them (1 Kings 14:11, 1 Kings 16:4). What the words promise, Gill says plainly, is that none of them will be buried. Henry observes how much of the sentence concerns the treatment of the body after death, and wonders whether such penalties were meant as figures of a worse misery for the soul; he also catches the sting in the repetition, that royal blood, however it swelled the veins with pride, would end as entertainment for scavengers.

Only now does the instigator get named, and Ellicott makes much of the delay. Throughout the rebuke the prophet has disdained to mention the woman onto whom the coward had no doubt shifted everything, so that the king stands exposed as the responsible party with no shred of covering left. The bolder criminal is dealt with in a sentence, and with a doom of shame that rarely falls on a woman but fits one who has forsworn the pity and modesty of her sex: thrown out as offal into the ditch beyond the wall, where the city refuse draws the half-wild scavengers of an Eastern town. Clarke reports the fulfilment at 2 Kings 9:36 as exact, and remarks that the bodies of poor Hindoos, and of those who have suffered public punishment, are still thrown into the rivers and eaten at the banks by dogs, vultures and crows.

Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that the two verses following are the compiler's own comment rather than more of the oracle, Ellicott adding that it takes its cue from the phrase about selling oneself. He finds in it contempt as much as condemnation: a most unkingly king, who sold himself to a course of crime he was half unwilling to take, against a conscience he did not disbelieve but merely ignored, and all for a paltry want; and who grovelled, besides, under the open rule of a wife, which to an Eastern reader accustomed to female intrigue but not female command would look especially monstrous.

Henry weighs the verdict against another. What was done to Uriah resembled this closely, yet David, that one matter excepted, did what was right, while here there was none like Ahab for ingenuity and industry in evil, who made a trade of it; the severity answers not to the vineyard alone but to a life of idolatry, which provoked God more than any immorality did. That his wife stirred him up excuses nothing, since the tinder was already in his own heart. Gill renders the idols he followed as dunghill gods, after the Tigurine version, and Ellicott notes that the comparison with the Amorites reaches past false worship to the nameless practices that always attended it. Clarke is briefest: the man hired himself out to the devil, and laboured at the work.
27:
The signs are conventional enough until the last of them. Clarke walks through the torn clothes, the hair garment next the skin, the fast, the nights lying in sackcloth, and reads each as evidence of something unfeigned. Over the closing phrase the versions part company. Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic make it barefoot; the Vulgate has the head hanging down; Houbigant turns it went groaning; Jarchi derives the word from being unshod, which Clarke thinks likeliest, and he hears in the slow measured tread the same note Aeschylus struck when the chorus was told to mourn the defeat of Xerxes with light and noiseless step. Ellicott surveys the same field and reaches the same verdict, that the Eastern versions and Josephus, with their barefoot, are far the most probable, though some Greek copies and the Latin agree on a bowed head instead.

What that walk was worth divides the witnesses as sharply as anything in the chapter. Clarke will allow no doubt at all: the king abased himself, the sorrow was real, and the divine approval settles the matter, since any measure of godly grief meets a proportionate regard from the Father of compassion. Delitzsch takes a more careful version of the same side, calling the remorse neither hypocritical nor merely outward, sincere though neither lasting nor productive of any real change, and resting the judgment on the fact that the Lord himself named it a humbling.

Gill will not have it. He reports the Jewish tradition generously, that the man prayed and fasted morning and evening, studied the law all his remaining days, never went back to his old works, and was truly converted; then he dismantles it. Nowhere is the queen rebuked for the murder. The vineyard is never returned to the dead man's family. The idols stay. Within a chapter the same king is taking counsel of four hundred prophets of the groves and saying plainly that he hates the one true prophet. What moved him, on this reading, was dread of the punishment rather than any fear of God, and yet Gill concedes what matters most, that nothing like it had been seen in any of his wicked predecessors and that heaven noticed it.

Henry calls him a kind of penitent, which is his way of granting the fact and refusing the substance. A proud hardened sinner was genuinely reduced, for God can make the stoutest heart tremble; but this was the dress and bearing of repentance, the garments torn and not the heart, and a hypocrite may travel a long way in the outward performance of holy duty and still fall short. The reprieve that follows Henry treats as a kind of pardon rather than a reversal: the sentence stands and only its execution is put off to the son. That such a man got anything at all shows a readiness to show mercy in which, as Bishop Sanderson put it, God would sooner be thought unholy or untrue or unjust, though he is none of these, than be thought unmerciful.

Ellicott holds the two halves together better than anyone. The outburst is exactly what an impressible temper would produce, and it might fairly be despised as too late and as the child of fear, more alive to the shame of being found out than to the shamefulness of the thing done. Human judgment would dismiss it. God finds in its very imperfection some germ of promise, and the partial remission proves the notice taken. The doom is not lifted; the king will still meet the end foretold, but he will die in honour, and the ruin of the house waits until his son has filled up the measure.
